title: Cannabis Chocolate 101: How Infused Chocolate Bars Work
h1: Cannabis Chocolate, Gummies and Mints: How Infused Sweets Work and How to Dose Them
metaDescription: How cannabis chocolate is made, why edibles feel different, how to dose a THC chocolate bar by the square, and how it compares with gummies and mints.
excerpt: Chocolate is the classic edible. Learn how infused bars are made, why digestion changes the effect, how to dose by the square, and how chocolate compares with gummies and mints.

body:
Cannabis chocolate is chocolate made with an activated cannabis ingredient, usually a refined THC oil or an infused fat, then molded into a bar, typically scored into equal squares that each hold a set amount of THC. Check the label for milligrams per square, use less than you expect to need, and be patient: eaten THC often takes 30 to 90 minutes to kick in. Here is how infused chocolate is made, why it feels different from smoking, how to dose it, and how it compares with gummies and mints.

## Why chocolate is a classic edible format

Chocolate and cannabis pair well for practical reasons:

- **Cannabinoids dissolve in fat,** and chocolate is rich in cocoa butter.
- **Cocoa has a strong flavor** that covers much of the plant's earthy taste.
- **A scored bar has built-in portions,** so dividing a dose is easy.

Chocolate has a long history in cannabis research too: an early study comparing ways of taking THC used a THC-laced chocolate cookie and found its effect lasted longer than smoking. For a wider look at formats, see our guide to [marijuana edibles](/blog/what-are-marijuana-edibles/).

## How cannabis chocolate is made: distillate or infused fat

Raw cannabis contains mostly THCA, which does not produce a high until heat converts it to THC, a step called decarboxylation. Chocolate makers start with an ingredient that has already been activated:

- **Distillate:** a refined, activated cannabis oil, measured by the milligram and blended into melted chocolate.
- **Infused fat:** cannabis-infused butter, cocoa butter or oil, more common in home kitchens.

The tricky part is spreading the dose evenly so every square carries the same amount. Commercial makers mix thoroughly and pour into scored molds, and Michigan products are tested before sale. Even so, research notes that THC content can vary within a single product and between batches, and Michigan labels state that actual THC and CBD values may vary by 10%.

Texture is part of the craft. Well-tempered chocolate snaps cleanly and holds its shape at room temperature, which keeps the score lines crisp and the squares easy to break. The infusion method affects flavor too: a refined distillate tastes mostly of chocolate, while an infused butter or oil tends to carry more of the plant's earthy notes.

## Digestion and 11-hydroxy-THC: why edibles feel different

When you smoke or vape, THC reaches your brain within minutes, peaks in about 20 to 30 minutes and tapers off within two to three hours. Eating it takes a longer route:

1. THC is absorbed through your gut and travels to your liver.
2. Liver enzymes convert part of it into 11-hydroxy-THC, a potent compound that readily reaches the brain.
3. More 11-hydroxy-THC forms after eating THC than after inhaling it, which may help explain why edibles can feel stronger and last longer.

The effects of an edible often begin 30 to 90 minutes after eating and peak around two to four hours, though your weight, metabolism and what you have eaten all shift the timing. Michigan labels also list an activation time. Those are typical ranges, not promises, which is why the classic mistake is taking more because the first piece "isn't working." Our post on [edible myths](/blog/myths-about-edibles/) clears up more misconceptions.

### Why the same square can feel different on different days

Research on eaten THC shows that the link between blood levels and how intoxicated people feel varies widely from person to person. In everyday terms, a square eaten after a big dinner may feel different from one eaten on an empty stomach, and your tolerance shifts with how often you use cannabis. Keep the variables steady while you learn: same dose, similar timing, no alcohol.

## Dosing by the square: mg per piece and per bar

Michigan caps adult-use edibles at 10 mg of THC per serving and 200 mg per package. A bar's label lists both numbers, and the math is simple: divide the bar's total THC by the number of squares.

| Bar total | Squares | THC per square | Half a square |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 mg | 10 | 5 mg | 2.5 mg |
| 100 mg | 10 | 10 mg | 5 mg |
| 100 mg | 20 | 5 mg | 2.5 mg |
| 200 mg | 20 | 10 mg | 5 mg |

Researchers have proposed 5 mg as a "standard THC unit," which makes a handy reference point. If you are new to edibles, start small, such as half of a 5 mg square, and give it at least two hours before having more. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) goes deeper.

A few habits help:

- Eat your square, then put the bar away, out of sight and out of reach.
- Do not combine edibles with alcohol.
- Never drive after using cannabis; Michigan bans driving under the influence.
- Talk with your doctor first if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, take medications, or have a health condition. Michigan labels carry a pregnancy and breastfeeding warning.

### Splitting a square and keeping track

To halve a square cleanly, chill the bar for a few minutes and cut along the score line with a sharp knife. Jot down the time and the amount you ate, then check in with yourself at the two-hour mark before deciding on more. A simple note on your phone beats guessing later.

### If you take more than you meant to

Stay put somewhere comfortable, sip water, have a non-infused snack and let time pass; effects fade as the hours go by. Do not drive. If someone has severe symptoms, such as chest pain or trouble breathing, call 911. For questions about an accidental or unexpected dose, Poison Control is at 1-800-222-1222.

## Chocolate vs. gummies vs. mints: onset, taste and portion control

Once swallowed, all three are absorbed through digestion, so the milligrams on the label and the listed activation time matter more than the format.

| Format | Portions | Taste and texture | Good to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chocolate | Scored squares | Rich; masks plant flavor well | Softens in heat; easy to split in half |
| Gummies | Individual pieces | Fruity or sour; chewy | Michigan bans human, animal and fruit shapes |
| Mints | Small pieces | Clean and minty | Small sizes suit low doses |

Michigan also keeps the word "candy" off edible packaging and requires opaque, child-resistant packages for every format. Check each product's activation time rather than assuming one format kicks in faster than another.

Dietary needs can settle the choice. Milk chocolate contains dairy, many gummies are made with gelatin, and nuts are common in chocolate production, so read the ingredient list if you avoid any of them. If you prefer less sugar, a small square of dark chocolate or a single mint may suit you better than a handful of gummies.

## Seasonal and limited flavors: what to check on the label

Seasonal and limited-run flavors come and go. Before you try one, check:

- **THC per square and per bar,** since a new flavor could be stronger or weaker than your usual bar
- **Serving size and scoring,** so you know what one portion looks like
- **Activation time** printed on the label
- **Ingredients and allergens,** such as milk, nuts or soy
- **The testing lab and test date,** plus the harvest date where listed
- **Michigan's universal THC symbol** on an intact, child-resistant package

Selection varies by store and changes often, so a flavor you saw once may not return. Planning something special? Our [Valentine's Day guide](/blog/cannabis-valentines-day-gift-guide/) includes infused chocolate strawberries with the dose math.

## Storage: heat, light, and keeping edibles away from kids and pets

- **Keep it cool and dark.** A hot car or sunny windowsill can melt a bar, and squares that lose their shape are harder to portion.
- **Keep it sealed** in its original child-resistant package, with the label intact.
- **Lock it up,** apart from regular sweets, where children cannot reach it or mistake it for a snack.

Over time, heat, light and air also break THC down; one of the compounds it turns into is CBN. White streaks on old chocolate, called bloom, come from heat or moisture changing the cocoa butter or sugar, which affects texture. Follow any date on the package and keep the bar sealed between servings.

Child exposures are a real risk. U.S. poison centers logged 207 cases of children under 6 eating cannabis edibles in 2017 and 3,054 in 2021; most happened at home, and about 23% of the children were admitted to a hospital. Pets are at risk too, and chocolate alone can make them sick. If someone eats an edible by accident, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or your veterinarian for a pet. Our guide to [storing cannabis](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) has more tips.

## Asking about edibles at a High Society store

Ask our budtenders to go over any edible's label with you: milligrams per piece and per package, activation time and ingredients. Tell us if you are new, and we will keep that in mind as we help you choose. Selection varies by store, so check with your [nearest High Society store](/dispensary-locations/). Adults 21 and older with valid ID, or 18 and older with a Michigan medical card, are welcome, and every Michigan store checks ID before each sale. Enjoy cannabis responsibly.

faq.q: How strong is a cannabis chocolate bar?
faq.a: It depends on the label. In Michigan, adult-use edibles can hold up to 10 mg of THC per serving and 200 mg per package, so a bar might be 100 mg split into ten 10 mg squares, or twenty 5 mg squares. Divide the total by the number of squares, and start with less than one serving if you are new.

faq.q: How long does a THC chocolate take to kick in?
faq.a: Often 30 to 90 minutes, with effects peaking around two to four hours after eating. Timing varies with your body, your metabolism and what else you have eaten, and Michigan labels list an activation time. Give it a full two hours before you decide on more.

faq.q: Are chocolate edibles stronger than gummies?
faq.a: No. Strength comes from the milligrams of THC, not the format. A 5 mg chocolate square and a 5 mg gummy contain the same amount of THC, and both pass through digestion and the liver. Differences you notice usually come down to dose, timing and what is in your stomach.

faq.q: How should I store cannabis chocolate?
faq.a: Keep it in its original child-resistant package in a cool, dark place, away from heat that can melt it, and lock it up. Store it apart from regular sweets, somewhere children and pets cannot get to it; chocolate alone is harmful to pets. If someone eats it by accident, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

faq.q: Can I make my own cannabis chocolate at home?
faq.a: Yes. Adults 21 and older can make it at home in Michigan with legally obtained cannabis, but home dosing is always an estimate. Potency depends on your starting material and on losses during decarboxylation and infusion, and mixing is rarely perfectly even. Label homemade chocolate clearly, start small and store it locked away.
